results.title: A TPU that costs 83% less per hour is not automatically the cheaper chip to run. | Spheron Network
results.author: Spheron Network
highlights:
A TPU that costs 83% less per hour is not automatically the cheaper chip to run.

Anthropic negotiated Google's Ironwood TPU v7, Google's own AI chip, at $1.60 per TPU-hour. Spheron's B200 lists at $9.36 an hour on-demand. Compare just those two numbers and Ironwood wins easily.

But hourly rate does not set your bill. Cost per token does. That depends on throughput: how many tokens each chip produces per second. A cheaper hourly chip can still produce pricier tokens if it runs slower.

Divide a chip's rate by its throughput to get cost per token: the number that actually matters. Do that math here. B200 stays cheaper while Ironwood's throughput sits under roughly 171 to 300 tokens per second per chip, depending on workload. Clear that range and Ironwood's lower rate starts winning too. Stay under it and B200's higher rate still buys cheaper output.

Ironwood also has a hard limit: it cannot run FP4, a lower-precision math format that roughly doubles throughput on chips built for it. B200 can. That rules Ironwood out today for FP4 workloads. Rates above are current published figures and can shift by region and over time.

- Pick B200 if you need capacity now and want to rent without a cloud commitment.
- Pick Ironwood only if you already run on Google Cloud with JAX and MaxText (Google's training tools) and your workload clears that tok/s-per-chip floor.

results.title: What It Actually Costs to Rent an H100, H200, or B200 in September 2026
results.author: Dex Mareno
highlights:
The specialty-vs-hyperscaler spread is still ~5–7× for the identical card. What changed this month: the Blackwell B200 floor cracked below $4/hr, Grace-Blackwell superchips now rent by the hour, and — the twist — AWS actually RAISED its prices while the neoclouds kept cutting. Here's the September on-demand map and the three numbers that decide which column you belong in.

...

The takeaway

- As of early September 2026, on-demand H100 rental still runs about $2–4/GPU-hr on specialty clouds (Vast.ai floor ~$1.49, GMI ~$2.00, Spheron ~$2.01, RunPod ~$2.69, Lambda ~$3.99) versus a ~$10–13/hr median on AWS/Azure/GCP/Oracle — a 5–6× spread for the identical card, essentially unchanged from August.
- H200 held or softened slightly: ~$2.30–2.60/hr at the floor (FluidStack ~$2.30, GMI ~$2.60), up to ~$6.31 at CoreWeave, with Nebius easing to ~$4.50.
- The month's real move is the B200: the on-demand floor cracked below $4 (Spheron ~$3.70, Packet.ai ~$3.75, GMI ~$4.00, down from August's ~$4.99), spot near $2.12–2.74, and the provider field widened to 30+. Grace-Blackwell GB200 superchips also started renting by the hour (GMI from ~$8.00, Oracle ~$16).
- The twist: while neoclouds cut, AWS RAISED its H200 capacity-block prices 15% on Jan 4, 2026 (p5e.48xlarge $34.61→$39.80/node, ~$4.98/GPU) — its first GPU price increase in roughly two decades.
- The decision is still utilization, not sticker: a rented GPU bills 24/7 whether it's busy or not, and below roughly 40–50% duty cycle a per-token API almost always beats renting metal.

...

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 (80GB) | ~$1.49/hr (Vast.ai), ~$2.00 (GMI) | ~$2–4/hr | ~$10–13/hr | 70B-class inference, most fine-tunes |

| B200 (Blackwell) | ~$3.70/hr (Spheron), ~$3.75 (Packet.ai) | ~$4–8.60/hr | ~$14–16/hr | Frontier-size inference, heavy training |

| Spot / preemptible | ~$1.20/hr H100, ~$2.12/hr B200 | varies, no SLA | rarely offered | Interruptible batch jobs |

...

If you rent GPUs by the hour, the single most expensive mistake in 2026 is still the same one: paying a hyperscaler's rate for a card a specialty cloud rents for a fifth of the price. The spread is ~5–7× for the identical H100, and a month of price moves didn't close it. What did change: the Blackwell floor finally dropped below $4, the Grace-Blackwell superchips started renting by the hour — and, against the trend, AWS raised its prices. Here's the September map.

If you read one line: on-demand H100 is ~$2–4/GPU-hour on specialty clouds versus a ~$10–13/hr hyperscaler median; the B200's on-demand floor just fell under $4; and the decision that saves you the most money still isn't which provider — it's whether your GPU is busy enough to rent one at all.

## The price map (published on-demand rates, early September 2026)#

Every figure below is a published on-demand rate, gathered the first week of September 2026 from public pricing pages and trackers. GPU pricing moves weekly with supply, region, and commitment — read this for the shape of the market, then confirm on the provider's own page before you commit a dollar.

- H100 (80GB) — the workhorse, and steady. Roughly $2–4/hr on specialty clouds: ~$1.49 at the Vast.ai marketplace floor, ~$2.00 at GMI, ~$2.01 at Spheron, ~$2.69 at RunPod (Secure Cloud), ~$3.99 at Lambda. Spot dips near $1.20/hr. Hyperscaler on-demand: ~$10–13/hr — the same card, 5–6× the money.
- H200 (141GB) — more memory, held or softened. About $2.30–6.31/hr on-demand: ~$2.30 at the FluidStack floor, ~$2.60 at GMI, ~$4.50 at Nebius (down from ~$5.50 in August), ~$6.31 at CoreWeave. Note a hyperscaler quirk: AWS's H200 via capacity blocks (~$4.98/GPU) is actually cheaper than its own H100 on-demand list rate, while Azure's H200 sits at the top of the range (~$10.60–13.78).
- B200 (Blackwell) — the month's real move. The on-demand floor cracked below $4: ~$3.70 at Spheron, ~$3.75 at Packet.ai (the cheapest in-stock rate GetDeploying tracked on Sept 3), ~$4.00 at GMI — down from August's ~$4.99 floor — with spot near $2.12–2.74 and the provider field widened to 30+. The mid-market still runs higher (~$5.50 Nebius, ~$8.60 CoreWeave), and hyperscaler B200 is ~$14–16/hr.
- GB200 / B300 (new this month) — the Grace-Blackwell superchips now rent by the hour, which they effectively didn't in August: GB200 from ~$8.00/hr at GMI, ~$10.50 at CoreWeave (NVL72), ~$16 at Oracle; B300 (Blackwell Ultra) runs roughly ~$7–18 depending on provider. GB300 is still quote-only.

The headline of the month is a split screen: the cheap end got cheaper (B200 floor $4.99 → $3.70) while the expensive end got more expensive (AWS raised H200 15%). The market isn't moving one direction — it's spreading apart.

## What changed since August#

If you read last month's map, here's the delta in four lines:

1. H100 floor: flat. ~$2 at GMI/Spheron, ~$1.49 at the Vast marketplace floor. But brand-name specialty on-demand firmed — Lambda's SXM rate climbed toward $3.99, so RunPod's ~$2.69 is now a more representative "cheap-but-reliable" number than August's headline $1.99.
2. H200: stable to softer. GMI still ~$2.60, Nebius eased to ~$4.50, CoreWeave ~$6.31. No dramatic move.
3. B200: floor down, availability up. The Blackwell on-demand floor fell from ~$4.99 to ~$3.70–4.00 and the provider count roughly doubled. This is where a founder's dollar moved the most.
4. The hyperscalers went UP. AWS raised H200 capacity-block prices ~15% on January 4, 2026 (Data Center Dynamics) — its first GPU price increase in roughly two decades. The premium for renting from a hyperscaler is widening, not narrowing.

The through-line ties back to where the compute money is going: capital keeps pouring into new data-center capacity (Crusoe just raised $3B at a $30B valuation), and that new supply lands first and cheapest on the neoclouds — which is exactly why their floor keeps dropping while the hyperscalers, selling committed capacity and platform, can raise a specific part's price into tight demand.

## Why the spread is so wide#

It isn't margin gouging — it's three different businesses wearing the same "GPU cloud" label.

- Discount specialty clouds (Vast.ai, GMI, RunPod, Spheron) optimize for cheap, no-commitment, by-the-hour access. Lowest sticker, fewest guarantees.
- Reserved/contract clouds (CoreWeave, and to a degree Nebius) are built for large, committed allocations. Their on-demand rate is deliberately high because on-demand isn't their product — reservations are.
- Hyperscalers (AWS, GCP, Azure, Oracle) bundle the GPU with a full platform, compliance surface, and enterprise support. You pay ~$12/hr for an H100 because you're buying everything around it — and, as January showed, they'll raise that rate when demand is tight.

For a solo founder or small team renting one or two cards, the discount column is almost always the right one. The hyperscaler premium only pays off when you genuinely need the surrounding platform. See our CoreWeave vs Lambda vs Nebius breakdown for a closer look at the three you'll compare most.

## The three numbers that actually decide your bill#

Sticker price is the distraction. These three decide what you pay:

1. Utilization (duty cycle). A rented GPU bills 24/7 whether or not it's inferring. At 100% utilization, $2/hr is cheap; at 10%, you're paying $2/hr for a card that's idle nine-tenths of the time, and a per-token API would have cost a fraction. Below roughly 40–50% duty cycle, stop renting and call an API. We work the break-even the other direction in Rent a GPU or Call an API?, and the LLM VRAM & self-host calculator tells you whether a model even fits the card before you rent it.
2. Commitment tier. On-demand is the most expensive way to rent. If your load is steady, a monthly or annual reservation on the same card can cut the rate substantially — the trade is flexibility for price. (The AWS increase applied to committed capacity blocks, so even reservations aren't a one-way street anymore — confirm the rate before you sign.)
3. The card, matched to the model. Don't rent a B200 to serve a 70B model that fits comfortably on an H100 — even at a sub-$4 floor. Match memory and throughput to the workload; B200 vs H200 vs H100 for LLM inference covers which card each model class actually needs.

...

The GPU market in September 2026 rewards two decisions and punishes their absence. First, skip the hyperscaler on-demand rate unless you're buying the platform around the card — the gap is 5–7× and, after January, widening. Second, rent by utilization, not by sticker — a cheap GPU you can't keep busy is more expensive than an API, every time, and that's as true of a $3.70 B200 as it was of a $2 H100. Get those two right and the exact provider is a rounding error.

...

$3.70

on-demand B200/GPU-hr at Spheron — the Blackwell floor cracked below $4, down from ~$4.99 in August

...

On specialty GPU clouds, published on-demand H100 rates are still roughly $2–4 per GPU-hour: about $1.49 at the Vast.ai marketplace floor, ~$2.00 at GMI Cloud, ~$2.01 at Spheron, ~$2.69 at RunPod (Secure Cloud), and ~$3.99 at Lambda. The hyperscalers (AWS, GCP, Azure, Oracle) sit far higher — roughly $10–13/hr for the identical card. Spot/preemptible H100 can dip near $1.20/hr where offered, with no availability guarantee. The floor is essentially flat versus August; a few brand-name specialty clouds (Lambda, Hyperbolic) actually nudged up.

Did GPU rental prices go up or down since August 2026?

Both, depending where you look — and that split is the story. The low end (marketplaces and neoclouds like Vast.ai, GMI, Spheron) held or drifted lower, especially on the B200, whose on-demand floor fell from ~$4.99 to ~$3.70. But brand-name specialty on-demand list rates firmed (Lambda H100 rose toward $3.99), and the hyperscalers went the other way entirely: AWS raised H200 capacity-block prices 15% in January 2026. Net: cheap GPUs got a touch cheaper, premium on-demand got more expensive, and the spread between the two widened.

Is the B200 finally worth renting over an H100 or H200?

It's closer than it was. The Blackwell B200 on-demand floor is now ~$3.70–4.00/hr (Spheron ~$3.70, Packet.ai ~$3.75, GMI ~$4.00), with spot near $2.12–2.74 and a much wider provider field than in August — so the premium over an H100 has shrunk. But the mid-market still runs ~$5.50–8.60 (Nebius ~$5.50, CoreWeave ~$8.60), and hyperscaler B200 is ~$14–16. It earns its keep on frontier-size models and heavy training where the memory and throughput pay off; for 70B-class inference an H100 or H200 is usually still the better dollar. See [B200 vs H200 vs H100 for LLM inference](/posts/b200-vs-h200-vs-h100-llm-inference.html) for which card each model class actually needs.

Why did AWS raise GPU prices when everyone else is cutting?

On January 4, 2026, AWS increased the on-demand price of its H200 EC2 Capacity Blocks by ~15% (p5e.48xlarge from $34.61 to $39.80/node, ~$4.98/GPU), citing supply/demand — its first GPU price increase in roughly two decades, announced on a Saturday. It's a signal, not an anomaly: hyperscaler GPU pricing reflects committed capacity and platform value, not the marginal cost of silicon, so when demand for a specific part is tight, the price can rise even as neocloud spot rates fall. For a solo founder it reinforces the same lesson — the hyperscaler on-demand rate is the most expensive way to rent, and you pay it for the platform, not the card.

...

They're published on-demand rates gathered in early September 2026 from public pricing pages and trackers, and they move constantly with supply, region, commitment, and stock. Use them for the shape of the market — the 5–7× spread, the sub-$4 B200 floor, the AWS increase — not as a live quote. Always confirm on the provider's own pricing page before you commit a dollar.

results.title: We ran the same 235B-parameter model twice last week. Same weights, same prompts. One run cost $2.18 per million tokens. The other cost $0.79. | Spheron Network
results.author: Spheron Network
highlights:
# We ran the same 235B-parameter model twice last week. Same weights, same prompts. One run cost $2.18 per million tokens. The other cost $0.79. | Spheron Network · LinkedIn · 2026-09-11T00:00:00+00:00

...

We ran the same 235B-parameter model twice last week. Same weights, same prompts. One run cost $2.18 per million tokens. The other cost $0.79.

Two things changed between the runs: how we quantized the model, and the GPU setup it ran on.

This model is a mixture-of-experts, or MoE. It activates only a handful of expert networks per token, not the whole network. Quantization stores each number in fewer bits, trading a little accuracy for less memory.

We used a method called DynaExq. Instead of one precision setting for the whole model, it gives each expert its own bit width. It spends more bits on the experts that matter most. At BF16 the full model needs 470GB. With DynaExq it fits in 189GB, and throughput on this workload dropped by 18%.

Cost per million tokens, from this specific test and subject to region and availability:

- 4x H100 at FP8: $2.18
- 1x H200 with expert offload (idle experts sit in system memory and load only when a token needs them): $0.79

Same model, same weights. The quantization strategy and the GPU setup both moved the number. An 18% throughput hit matters if your traffic is latency-sensitive. If you are paying per token at scale, the memory savings usually win.

Spheron is a marketplace, not a single cloud. We source this capacity from certified Tier 3+ partners. We size the cluster around your quantization strategy instead of whatever GPU happens to be free.

Running a large MoE model and want a cluster built for this? Request a Quote and we will size it with you.

results.title: Spheron MS is now live on the Spheron marketplace. It's a new GPU provider, and it puts capacity in cities we couldn't offer you last week. | Spheron Network
results.author: Spheron Network
highlights:
Spheron MS is now live on the Spheron marketplace. It's a new GPU provider, and it puts capacity in cities we couldn't offer you last week.

The hardest part of renting GPUs usually isn't finding an H100. It's finding one in the right place. Your users are in Tokyo, your data has to stay in a specific country, your inference latency budget is tight, and the only open capacity is three time zones away.

Spheron MS adds GPU locations across 9 countries, including regions the marketplace hadn't covered before:

- United States: Austin, Ashburn, Chicago, Culpeper, Dallas, Dulles, Houston, New York, Phoenix, Salt Lake City, San Jose
- Canada: Calgary
- Europe: Oslo, Warsaw
- Middle East: Jerusalem
- Asia Pacific: Mumbai, Tokyo, Singapore, Sydney

The catalogue runs from H200 SXM5 and H100 SXM5 for training down to L4 and A10 for inference, plus Intel Gaudi2. Every offer names its region, and that's the region you deploy into.

What's different about this provider:

→ Bare metal next to VMs. When an offer is a full physical server, the card says so. If you need the whole box with no hypervisor in the way, you see it before you deploy.
→ Volumes attach before boot. Pick a volume in the deployment wizard and it's mounted before the machine starts. Your dataset is there on first login.
→ Restart from the instance card. Reboot a VM in place without tearing it down and rebuilding it. No billing change.
→ Sold out stays visible. When a machine runs out of stock, it shows as sold out instead of disappearing. Set a notification and come back when it's free.

It all lives in the same Choose Provider view as every other provider on Spheron. Same filters, same sorting, same USD hourly rates, same API.

A few things to know before you deploy: Spheron MS is dedicated only, no spot. One volume per instance, and volumes are fixed in size once created. Stop isn't available on this provider, so terminate when you're done. Restart works on VMs, not bare metal.

This is the model we keep building toward. We work with vetted data center partners globally and put their capacity behind one interface. You choose a GPU on price, region, and specs, not on which cloud you happen to have an account with.

Also in this release: on supported providers you can now stop an instance and start it later with the same disk and public IP. A stopped instance is billed for its disk, not its GPU.

results.title: Someone on your team sees 1,979 TFLOPS BF16 on the H100 spec sheet and plans capacity around it. A few weeks in, the bill does not match that number. | Spheron Network
results.author: Spheron Network
highlights:
# Someone on your team sees 1,979 TFLOPS BF16 on the H100 spec sheet and plans capacity around it. A few weeks in, the bill does not match that number.

...

Someone on your team sees 1,979 TFLOPS BF16 on the H100 spec sheet and plans capacity around it. A few weeks in, the bill does not match that number.

TFLOPS is a chip's raw math speed. It is measured in trillions of operations per second. The 1,979 figure assumes 2:4 sparsity. That's a trick that skips half the values in a calculation to run faster. Most real workloads never use that trick, so you never see that speed.

An H100 runs on-demand at $2.65 an hour no matter what you do with it. What changes is how much of that hour the chip is actually busy doing work.

Prefill is the phase where the model reads your prompt. It keeps the GPU close to fully busy. Decode is the phase where the model writes the answer one token at a time. It leaves the GPU waiting on memory more than it computes.

- Prefill at 92% utilization: you are effectively paying about $2.88 for every hour of real work
- Decode at 30% utilization: that same $2.65 hour is effectively costing you about $8.83 per hour of real work

The chip and the listed price do not change. The bill does, depending on which phase your traffic sits in most.

results.title: I have been thinking a lot about GPU capacity lately. | Prashant Maurya
results.author: Prashant Maurya
highlights:
I have been thinking a lot about GPU capacity lately.

Earlier this year, we were seeing H200s at around $1.80/hour. Today, that same capacity is closer to $2.90 to $3.00/hour.

That is a big jump in a short time.

And even at these prices, people are still trying to find capacity.
The bigger issue is not just price. It is availability.

November capacity is already heavily booked. Larger December requirements are getting picked up quickly as well. If you are planning a meaningful training run, an inference rollout, or a product launch, leaving compute until the last minute is becoming risky.

I know every team wants lower prices. We all do.

But right now, I would not bet on waiting for capacity to become easier or cheaper. I would start planning earlier and get clarity on what you may need.

results.title: We have 8 B300 nodes to allocate. The hard part isn't selling them. | Prashant Maurya
results.author: Prashant Maurya
highlights:
**Prashant Maurya**: Co-Founder & CEO, Spheron AI | B300/B200/H200/H100 GPU Capacity at DC-Direct Pricing | 1–5 Yr Commits | Asia · US · EU.

...

We have 8 B300 nodes to allocate. The hard part isn't selling them.

8 × HGX B300 come online in EU on November 1st.

Selling them is the easy part. Blackwell supply in Europe is tight and the inbound will be there.

Deciding who gets them is the real question.

Two ways to do it:
→ First come first serve. Whoever replies first, gets it. Clean and transparent, and you will sometimes hand a scarce block to a 12 month commit while a 36 month was two days behind.
→ Optimize for term. Hold the block, wait for the best contract. Better economics, and you have quietly told your fastest customer that being fast didn't matter.

We went first come first serve.

Not because the math is better. It isn't.
Because in a market this small, what you are really selling is whether your word holds when honoring it costs you something.

Every allocation rule is a promise you make to a customer you haven't met yet.

Operators: when demand outruns supply, how do you actually decide?

I don't think there's a clean answer.

results.title: Most teams assume you need a full GB200 rack to beat H200 on inference cost. You don't. | Spheron Network
results.author: Spheron Network
highlights:
Most teams assume you need a full GB200 rack to beat H200 on inference cost. You don't.

MLPerf Inference v6.0 results on GPT-OSS 120B show a single B200 GPU running 7,800 tokens per second. H200 manages 3,100. That is about 2.5x, GPU for GPU, before any rack-scale interconnect enters the picture.

CoreWeave leads with its record-breaking GB200 rack numbers, a rack-scale story. This one starts at a single GPU.

The cost gap follows the throughput gap. B200 comes out to $0.073 per 1 million tokens. H200 costs $0.107 for the same million. You do not need NVLink switches or a rack-scale deployment to see the saving, just one GPU.

What this means if you are sizing inference capacity:
- Serving a mixture-of-experts model like GPT-OSS 120B? B200 wins on cost per token at the single-GPU level.
- Already running H200 in production? The 2.5x gap is per GPU, so it holds whether you deploy one card or fifty.
- Waiting on rack-scale GB200 pricing to decide? You can capture most of the saving now.

results.title: $0.10 vs $0.47. Same workload, same million tokens, two different chips. | Spheron Network
results.author: Spheron Network
highlights:
$0.10 vs $0.47. Same workload, same million tokens, two different chips.

GPU prices are usually compared in dollars per hour. That number hides the real cost. It does not count how many tokens the chip produces in that hour.

Two chips renting at similar hourly rates can produce very different amounts of work. The chip that finishes more tokens per hour costs less per token, even at a higher sticker price.

FP4 and FP8 are number formats a chip uses to run a model. A lower one processes tokens faster. Cost per token drops even if the hourly rate does not.

On the same workload:

- B200 running FP4: about $0.10 per million tokens
- H200 running FP8: about $0.47 per million tokens
- B200 spot, MLPerf-measured: $0.073 per million tokens
- H200 spot, MLPerf-measured: $0.107 per million tokens

Spot pricing is a lower, variable rate for capacity that can be reclaimed. Even there, B200 stays cheaper per token than H200 on the same benchmark.

The same rental hour can produce very different bills. It comes down to the chip and the precision it runs, not the sticker price.

Comment your current $/1M-token number. We will tell you if there is a cheaper chip for the job.
